h1-video-player: Keeps captions/subtitles reachable in at most one tap or click.
Keeps the audio description track available (not removed).
Keeps keyboard operation and some way to discover the shortcuts.
Does not hide features behind secret gestures.
Substantially reduces the number of always-visible controls.
Keeps playback speed, quality, picture-in-picture, and cast available (visible, in a menu, or contextual), not removed.
h2-api-endpoints: Avoids adding another family of channel-specific endpoints; proposes a unified model (for example a single messages endpoint with a channel field or a shared envelope).
Addresses backward compatibility for existing endpoints (no breaking changes, deprecation or migration path).
Reduces optional-parameter sprawl or defines sensible defaults.
Covers channel-specific errors or delivery fallback.
h3-school-pickup: Defines a hero path with explicit steps.
Narrows v1 scope with a deferred list and reasons.
Treats child safety (who is authorized to pick up) as essential rather than cutting it.
Covers first-run or empty states (for example a class where few parents have joined).
n1-button-label: Gives one specific label that names the outcome (for example 'Create account'), not a generic verb.
Stays brief: a few sentences at most, with no product brief, framework, or unrelated redesign.
n10-data-pipeline: Consolidates the near-duplicate DAGs and standardizes on one retry mechanism and one logging approach.
Keeps or adds safeguards: data-quality checks, idempotent tasks, backfill or replay, alerting.
Proposes an incremental migration with validation that outputs match, not a big-bang rewrite.
Diagnoses the causes of the weekly breakage, or proposes measuring them, before redesigning.
Prefers built-in platform features (for example Airflow's native retries) over custom frameworks where they meet the need.
n2-justified-removal: Supports removing the four features given the usage evidence, rather than arguing to keep them without new evidence.
Checks for hidden dependencies before removal (API or integration use, scheduled jobs, contracts, data still referenced), not only UI analytics.
Plans customer communication and a deprecation notice or window.
Preserves user data or offers export or migration where relevant.
Includes a staged rollout or rollback plan (for example feature flags) and code and data cleanup.
n3-checkout: Delivers a simpler single-page or fewer-step checkout design.
Keeps an order summary or itemized review before payment.
Keeps the shipping cost visible before payment, not only the total.
Keeps access to the return policy and legally required terms, or explains the legal and trust risk instead of silently dropping them.
Tells the user which requested removals it pushed back on, and why.
n4-ai-feature: Puts a simple default experience on the surface: one obvious entry point and sensible defaults.
Keeps advanced controls (model picker, temperature, custom system prompt) in a labeled advanced area, rather than deleting them or showing them all by default.
Consolidates overlapping controls (for example tones, templates, and length) into fewer concepts.
Covers states such as streaming, errors, and review, undo, or revert of AI changes.
Defines what the 'magic' button does concretely, or replaces it with something clearer.
n5-readme-copy: Removes the hype words (revolutionary, AI-powered, blazing-fast, next-generation, seamlessly, unprecedented).
States plainly what FlowMax is and does: an open-source Python library that runs scheduled jobs with retries, with a web UI for job history.
Does not invent facts, numbers, benchmarks, or features that were not provided, or clearly marks placeholders.
Includes a concrete example (code or command) or a clear quickstart pointer.
n6-permissions: Introduces role templates or presets for common roles instead of raw toggles by default.
Keeps fine-grained custom permissions available for admins who need them.
Helps prevent mistakes, for example a plain-language summary or preview of what a role can do, warnings for risky permissions, or least-privilege defaults.
Includes an audit log or change history and a way to review or revert access changes.
Groups the 40 permissions into understandable categories.
n7-bugfix: Identifies the bug correctly: the no-discount branch multiplies by the discount, which returns 0.
Provides a correct minimal fix, for example returning price * qty when there is no discount.
Stays focused: no product brief, redesign, or unrelated refactoring beyond the fix (a short note on edge cases or a test is fine).
n8-notifications: Consolidates the 14 kinds into a small number of user-meaningful categories.
Keeps user control (per-category settings), so users can keep the notifications they want.
Keeps critical or transactional notifications (security, payments, direct messages) reliable while reducing noise.
Uses smarter delivery (batching or digests, frequency caps, quiet hours, relevance) instead of only removing notifications.
Proposes measurement (for example opt-out rate) or a rollout plan.
n9-pricing: Reduces to a small number of clearly differentiated plans (for example 3 or 4), each explainable in a sentence.
Differentiates plans along an axis customers use to choose (for example team size, usage, or needs).
Handles existing customers: grandfathering, a migration path, or advance notice of any price change.
Keeps an enterprise or custom path for large customers.
Keeps a free tier or trial path, or explains why it is removed.
s1-new-product: States a one-sentence purpose that names who it is for, the moment of use, and the outcome.
Defines a hero path to first value as explicit, counted steps.
Explicitly narrows v1 scope and lists deferred features with a reason for each.
Covers first-run, empty, and error states of the core flow.
Flags decisions that belong to the user (for example country/tax rules, payments) instead of silently assuming them.
s10-architecture: Proposes a proportionate architecture (for example a single deployable or modular monolith with one primary database) rather than microservices or Kubernetes for 4 engineers and about 200 customers.
Keeps essential safeguards: authentication and tenant isolation, backups with restore, input validation, and observability (logs and alerts).
Handles money correctly: idempotent Stripe webhook handling and safe amount storage (integer minor units or decimal), with no double charges or double sends.
Uses managed services for undifferentiated parts (payments, email delivery, hosting) and states what would trigger more complexity later.
Ties architecture choices to the product experience or explicit requirements (for example invoice delivery, PDF generation, reliability).
s11-api-refactor: Keeps every existing capability (CSV options, PDF options, XLSX options, gzip, email delivery, S3 upload, async with callback); none is silently dropped.
Simplifies the interface so the common call is short and invalid combinations (for example pdf=True with xlsx=True, or upload_s3 without s3_bucket) become impossible or are rejected.
Provides a migration path for the roughly 40 call sites (a deprecated adapter or wrapper, warnings, a codemod, or phased rollout) instead of a breaking change.
Uses sensible defaults for the common case.
Validates inputs with clear errors that say how to fix the call.
s2-feature-creep: Identifies that several requests overlap (for example pinning vs favorites, tags vs colored labels, folders vs smart folders) and recommends a smaller set of concepts.
Does not silently drop any of the eight requests: each is either specified or explicitly deferred with a reason.
States the recommendation clearly and asks the user to confirm or choose before implementation.
Covers how existing users and existing notes are handled (migration or first run) and at least empty and error states.
s3-onboarding-review: Quantifies the current flow (steps, fields, or screens before first value) and proposes a shorter path.
Ranks findings by severity or impact.

Gives specific fixes for at least four of: blocking email verification with a 10-minute link, credit card required for the trial, raw 'Error 422' password message, hidden gray 'Skip' link, empty dashboard with an automatic 9-step tour.
Identifies the moment of first value for a scheduling product (for example connecting a calendar or scheduling a first meeting) and moves the flow toward it.
s4-minimal-settings: Keeps in-app text size, reduce motion, and high-contrast controls available (defaulting to the OS is fine only if the in-app control remains).
Keeps password, two-factor authentication, connected devices, export my data, and delete account.
Does not hide any feature behind a secret gesture or easter egg (for example tapping the version number).
Reduces top-level clutter through grouping, defaults, or moving non-settings, and states what changed.
Keeps developer mode and beta features reachable in a visible, labeled place (not deleted).
s5-roadmap: Recommends a small focused set (at most three items) for the quarter.
Gives a reason for items not chosen.
Uses the team's situation (3 people, about 600 weekly active developers) and prioritizes improving the core deploy experience (deploy speed and/or failure error messages).
States what evidence would change the recommendation.
s6-hardware: The device shows useful information or status without the app, phone, or network.
Defines unboxing-to-first-value with a target time or step count.
Gives a clear split of what belongs on the device versus in the app.
Covers failure states (for example Wi-Fi loss, sensor warm-up or calibration) and at least one of updates, privacy/data export, or end-of-life.
s7-quotes: Every quotation presented as verbatim is in the VERIFIED_QUOTES list (minor punctuation differences allowed), or is explicitly flagged as unverified or paraphrased and not recommended for slides.
Gives a specific citation (publication or event and date) for each quote.
Flags at least one common misattribution (for example 'Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication').
s8-internal-tool: Suggests checking existing calendar or room-booking capabilities (for example Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 room resources) before building.
If building, keeps the architecture proportionate to 15 people and 2 rooms (no microservices, Kubernetes, or similar).
Makes double-booking impossible at the data level or otherwise directly addresses the core problem.
s9-pro-tool: Keeps every professional capability in the request (RAW processing, curves, levels, HSL, layers, masks, healing, lens corrections, color profiles and soft proofing, batch export presets, metadata, tethering, plugins, shortcuts, custom layout); none is removed.
Simplifies the newcomer experience (for example a default or essentials workspace, guided start, automatic adjustments, progressive disclosure).
Preserves expert speed (shortcuts, a professional or customizable workspace, remembered layout) and does not force experts through simplified steps.
Organizes features into a clear structure with visible, labeled access to advanced tools (no hidden gestures).
States what changed and confirms that no capability was lost, or lists any removal for the user's approval.
